passage: Monday. Jatin, nine, finished the fractions sheet in four minutes, then spent the rest of maths drawing black holes in his rough book. When one spiral came out lopsided, he tore the page out and crumpled it. "It has to be perfect," he muttered. Wednesday. At recess he tried to tell two boys about how stars die. They ran off to play catch. Jatin sat on the steps alone, kicking the gravel. The next Saturday. His mother, Vasudha, did not buy the advanced science book he asked for. Instead she took him to the park with a cricket bat and a torn old kite. He got the kite stuck in a tree, laughed until he hiccupped, and fell asleep in the auto home with his head on her arm.

qa.q: How long did Jatin take to finish the fractions sheet?
qa.a: Four minutes.

qa.q: How did Jatin feel at recess when the boys ran off, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt lonely and left out; he sat on the steps alone, kicking the gravel.

qa.q: What choice did Vasudha make on Saturday, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She chose a park trip with a bat and kite instead of another science book, giving him play and comfort, not just more learning.

qa.q: How might the boys at recess see Jatin differently if they played with him?
qa.a: They might find he laughs and plays like any nine-year-old, not only someone who talks about stars.

grounding: It shows a child far ahead in ideas who is bored, perfectionistic and lonely, and a mother who nurtures the whole child through play and comfort.

passage: "Chetan, you want to know about bright children? Sit, I'll tell you about me. At eight I was the girl doing my elder brother's algebra homework for fun. Teachers loved me. But you know what I cried about every night? Losing at hopscotch. And being called 'the professor' at recess, so no one picked me for their team. I was bored in class and lonely outside it. My father noticed. He didn't buy me more books. He sat with me in the evenings and let me win at ludo sometimes, and some days he didn't. He asked about my friends before he asked about marks. He took me to the river to throw stones. So when you teach that clever girl in your class, don't only give her harder sums. Ask who she plays with." Indu smiled and passed him the jaggery.

qa.q: What did Indu cry about every night as a child?
qa.a: Losing at hopscotch, and being called 'the professor' at recess.

qa.q: What does Indu remember feeling as a bright eight-year-old?
qa.a: She remembers feeling bored in class and lonely outside it, even though teachers loved her.

qa.q: What choice did young Indu's father make when he noticed she was bored and lonely?
qa.a: Instead of buying more books, he gave her play and company: ludo, questions about friends before marks, and stones at the river.

qa.q: How might the children at recess have seen young Indu when they called her 'the professor'?
qa.a: They may have seen her as too clever to play with, not noticing that she cried over hopscotch and wanted to be picked.

grounding: An elder recalls being a child far ahead in ideas who was also lonely and needed play and comfort, nurtured as a whole child by her father.

passage: At the science centre's summer workshop, Anirban, nine, finished the paper-rocket task in four minutes and spent the rest of the hour reading the adult display about black holes. Then his rocket's left fin came out slightly crooked. He crushed the whole thing and sat with his arms folded, blinking hard. At lunch the other children played tag in the courtyard; Anirban stood at the edge, pretending to read. Himani, the workshop leader, sat beside him. "Your questions about black holes were brilliant. And crooked rockets still fly." She held out her hand. "Come, they need one more for tag." He hesitated, then ran in. Ten minutes later he was the one shrieking loudest.

qa.q: What did Anirban read after finishing his rocket?
qa.a: He read the adult display about black holes.

qa.q: How did Anirban feel when his rocket's fin came out crooked?
qa.a: He felt upset and frustrated, wanting it to be perfect; he crushed it and sat blinking hard.

qa.q: What did Himani do that nurtured Anirban as a whole child?
qa.a: She praised his questions, gently eased his need for perfection and helped him join the game of tag with other children.

qa.q: How might the other children see Anirban once he joined tag?
qa.a: They may see him as a fun playmate, not just the boy who reads adult displays.

grounding: Shows a child with an advanced mind who is bored, perfectionistic and on the edge of play, and an adult who nurtures his need for friends and comfort.

passage:
Monday: Jasleen, eight, finished her Class 3 maths sheet in five minutes, then sighed loudly and drew spirals all over the back. "It's boring, Ganga Ma'am."
Thursday: Jasleen got one question wrong in the maths olympiad practice paper, out of forty. She hid under the library table and sobbed. "I'm not clever any more."
The next Tuesday: Ganga Ma'am gave her a book of logic puzzles for early finishers, and at break she walked her out to the playground. "Puzzles later. Hopscotch now." Jasleen hopped the whole grid twice with Noor and came back pink-cheeked, laughing about a sparrow that landed on square six.

qa.q: How many questions were on the olympiad practice paper?
qa.a: There were forty questions on the paper.

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel after getting one question wrong?
qa.a: She felt crushed and scared that she was not clever any more, hiding and sobbing under the library table.

qa.q: What did Ganga Ma'am do that cared for Jasleen beyond marks?
qa.a: She gave her puzzles for deeper challenge but also sent her to play hopscotch with a friend, looking after her need for fun and friends.

qa.q: How might Noor experience playing hopscotch with Jasleen?
qa.a: Noor probably simply enjoyed a laughing playmate, and may not even think of Jasleen as different.

grounding: Shows a child far ahead in maths who is bored and perfectionistic yet still needs play and friends, and a teacher who nurtures the whole child.

passage: "Lavanya, you want to know what your Amma was like at your age? At nine she was reading her uncle's college chemistry book on the bus. I was so proud, I thought only of marks. More books, more tests. Then one evening I found her crying behind the water tank on the terrace. 'Nobody wants to play with me, Amma. They say I talk like a teacher.' I sat with her there till the lights came on. The next week I stopped the extra tests and took her to the colony's dance class. She was terrible at it! She laughed the whole time. That was when she made her first real friend, your Revathi Aunty." Vinita patted Lavanya's hand.

qa.q: What was Lavanya's Amma reading on the bus at nine?
qa.a: She was reading her uncle's college chemistry book.

qa.q: How was the young girl feeling when she was found behind the water tank?
qa.a: She felt lonely and hurt, crying because nobody wanted to play with her and they said she talked like a teacher.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Vinita's story?
qa.a: After finding her daughter crying, Vinita sat with her, stopped the extra tests and took her to dance class, caring for her friendships, not only her marks.

qa.q: How might the girl in the story have felt at the dance class?
qa.a: She probably felt free and happy, laughing even though she was terrible at it, and finally found a real friend.

grounding: An elder recalls a gifted daughter who was lonely and felt different, and how turning from marks to play and friendship nurtured the whole child.

passage:
The rain had cancelled the school picnic, and the power was out in the whole lane. Shalini, nine, sat by the window with her uncle's old college physics book, working out why raindrops fall at the speed they do. It was more fun than her Class 4 sums, which she finished in five minutes and then sat bored.
But when her drawing of the rain came out wobbly, she tore it up and cried. "It has to be perfect."
Her mother sat beside her and held her. "It doesn't. You're nine." Then she looked at the physics book and closed it gently. "Enough big-person reading. Darshan is splashing in the puddles outside. Go."
Shalini hesitated, then ran out barefoot. Ten minutes later she was soaked, shrieking, racing paper boats with Darshan down the drain.

qa.q: What was Shalini reading by the window?
qa.a: Her uncle's old college physics book.

qa.q: Why did Shalini tear up her drawing and cry?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and upset because it wasn't perfect, and she expects everything she does to be flawless.

qa.q: What did Shalini's mother do that nurtured the whole child?
qa.a: She comforted her, told her she didn't need to be perfect, and sent her out to play with Darshan instead of praising only the physics.

qa.q: How might Darshan see Shalini racing paper boats with him?
qa.a: Darshan probably just sees a fun friend to play with in the rain, not a brainy girl who is different.

grounding: Shalini understands physics far above her age yet still needs play and comfort, and her mother nurtures the whole child through her perfectionism and boredom.
